extracted.intended_audience: developmental psychologists, cognitive scientists, and researchers designing child humor/ToM experiments
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating behavioral tasks that measure 4–5-year-old children's recognition of slapstick humor (categorizing misfortune scenes as funny) and its relation to Theory of Mind and emotion-recognition abilities. Includes stimulus design, scoring, participant criteria, and statistical analysis guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of slapstick humor (comic vs affective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Children recognize and categorize a misfortunate situation as funny only if the victims show a funny bewildered face (slapstick humor), and not a painful or angry expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized in the study as a forced-choice between a comic (bewildered/funny face) and an affective (angry/painful face) picture; correct = choosing the comic picture. The predicted probability of recognizing comic pictures should exceed chance level (50%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage theory of humor processing (incongruity + resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor processing involves first detecting an incongruity that violates expectations and second resolving that incongruity, which produces amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In slapstick, the victim's bewildered facial expression serves as a signal of incongruity and harmlessness, facilitating the cognitive reinterpretation that leads to humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slapstick humor characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Slapstick is characterized by physical and nonverbal comedy involving misfortunate situations, clownish behavior, and anthropomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stimuli should depict misfortunes (e.g., falling, spilling) and manipulate the victim's facial expression (bewildered/funny vs angry/painful) to test recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association with Theory of Mind (ToM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Children's recognition of slapstick humor is hypothesized and tested to be associated with their Theory of Mind abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure ToM (here via the Children's Social Understanding Scale, CSUS); analyze whether higher ToM scores predict better humor recognition (one SD increase in ToM related to increased odds of correct recognition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to facial emotion recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether humor recognition is related to the ability to recognize facial emotional expressions (happy, sad, fearful, angry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure emotion recognition separately (forced-choice task) and test each emotion's recognition score as a predictor of humor recognition; note that absence of a relation may reflect ceiling effects or context dependence of emotion recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-related developmental expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor recognition is expected to increase with age according to developmental theories (e.g., McGhee stages), with 2–7 years (Stage 3) appreciating slapstick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for age as a predictor and compare predicted probabilities across the age range; however, in a narrow 4–5-year window age effects may be non-significant and ToM may explain more variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant inclusion/exclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude children with developmental disorder, impaired sight, preterm birth, or being bi- or multilingual from the sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define and screen these criteria during recruitment to ensure sample homogeneity for the targeted developmental window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulus balancing
rubrics_metrics.description: People depicted in each pair of images should be balanced for gender, age, and body parts involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stimulus sets where each factor is counterbalanced across comic/affective alternatives to avoid confounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion recognition task design
rubrics_metrics.description: Present four pictures (2 female, 2 male actors) each displaying one of four emotions (happiness, sadness, fear, anger) and ask the child to point to the target emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Task consisted of 24 randomized trials with pseudo-counterbalanced actor targets so each actor served as the target for each emotion at least once; score 1 for correct selection, 0 otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor recognition task design (timing & structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a practice trial followed by test trials presenting pairs (one comic, one affective) in randomized blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study: one practice pair shown for 2,000 ms; test trials: fixation cross 250 ms, stimuli shown 6,000 ms, fixation cross 250 ms, then auditory prompt; total of 32 test trials presented in four blocks of six and one block of eight, with randomized order. Between blocks show a neutral image (elephant) as a pause. Record parent's keypress corresponding to child's pointing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forced-choice response scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Each trial is scored binary: 1 if the child chooses the comic picture (for humor task) or the correct emotion (for emotion task), 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate scores as percentage correct; note forced-choice may measure relative funniness rather than absolute amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parents register responses protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents present during online testing are instructed to register which picture their child points to by clicking or pressing keys, and not to alter responses based on their own judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit instructions to parents are necessary to reduce parental influence, though parent-report elements (e.g., CSUS) remain subjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial randomization and counterbalancing
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomize presentation order of blocks and trials; pseudo-counterbalance actors and target positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomization avoids order effects; ensure each actor/condition appears appropriately across trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centering and scaling continuous predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Center and scale predictors (e.g., Age, ToM, emotion recognition scores) to z-scores to facilitate model fit and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardize predictors before entering into mixed models; report what 0 and 1 SD represent for interpretation of plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized linear mixed model specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Model humor recognition per trial as a binary outcome using a GLMM with predictors (Age_scaled, ToM_scaled, happy_scaled, sad_scaled, fearful_scaled, angry_scaled) and random intercepts for Participant and trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use binomial family with logit link. The authors included only random intercepts (no random slopes) due to convergence and theoretical considerations. Report R notation and check residuals and random effect distributions for normality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random effects choices and convergence considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Include participant-level random intercepts to account for baseline differences and consider trial-level random intercepts; avoid random slopes if the model fails to converge or lacks theoretical justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test model fit; if random slopes cause non-convergence, simplify to intercepts only and report rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing against chance (50%) using CI bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval for predicted probability exceeds chance level (50% for binary forced-choice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use predicted probabilities with CIs to determine if performance is significantly above chance across age/ToM ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and reporting of pre-registration and open data
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-register study design and analysis plan and make anonymized data and analysis scripts available (e.g., OSF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-registration increases transparency; link to OSF repository and report software/packages used for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of ToM via parent-report CSUS (limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Children's Social Understanding Scale (CSUS) as a parent-report measure of ToM, acknowledging it is valid and reliable but subjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider combining parent-report with direct behavioral ToM measures in future studies to reduce reliance on subjective reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of eye-tracking/gaze data quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect gaze data where possible but exclude it from analysis if calibration and data quality are deficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report that eye-tracking was attempted and justify exclusion due to low quality; consider technical solutions to improve calibration in online child samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics, consent, and participant compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain ethics approval, follow Helsinki Declaration standards, secure informed consent from guardians, and offer modest compensation (certificate and small present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document ethics committee approval and consent procedures; report recruitment source and compensation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting standards and statistical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Report descriptive statistics (N, mean, SD, min, max), model summaries (odds ratios, CI, p-values), random effects variance, ICC, number of observations, marginal/conditional R2, and visualization of residuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard software (R packages: lme4, sjPlot, rstatix, emmeans) and report CI calculation method; bold p-values < 0.05 and visualize predicted probabilities with 95% CIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of forced-choice and design choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Forced-choice design may lead children to select the 'funnier' alternative rather than indicate absolute amusement; behavioral outputs (smiles/laughter) were not measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge this limitation in interpretation and consider adding direct measures of amusement and broader emotion categories in future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations for future experimental improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Include additional emotions (e.g., surprise, disgust), behavioral ToM assessments, neurophysiological measures (EEG), and control conditions to clarify mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose follow-up experiments with richer emotion sets, EEG measures of N170/N220/N400, and control stimuli (e.g., disconcerted expression in non-comic condition) to better isolate facial-expression effects.
